html:
The mining of phosphate rock on the small Pacific island of Nauru, which began in 1906 and stripped most of its interior. For a time it made Nauru one of the richest countries per person in the world, and then left it broke.

The rich phosphate, formed over ages from the droppings of seabirds, was found in 1900 by Albert Ellis of the Pacific Islands Company, who had noticed a piece of Nauru rock used as a doorstop in Sydney. Mining began under German rule in 1906. After the First World War Nauru was run by Britain, Australia and New Zealand, whose British Phosphate Commissioners shipped the rock as cheap fertiliser to their farms. The same company mined nearby Banaba, whose people were later moved to Rabi in Fiji.

Nauru became independent in 1968 and took over the mines in 1970. The money brought high incomes for a while, but much of the trust fund was lost on bad investments, and the phosphate was nearly gone by 2000. Some 80 percent of the island is now a wasteland of coral pinnacles. Nauru later hosted a detention centre for asylum seekers sent by Australia.
